title: Landslide in Mumbai's Kurla Kills Six as Monsoon Rains Paralyze India's Financial Capital
excerpt: Heavy monsoon rainfall triggered a deadly landslide in Kurla and forced closures of the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, flights, and train services across the city.
body:
• At least six people were killed and two injured after a landslide struck Mumbai's Kurla area on August 12, triggered by torrential monsoon rainfall.
  • The India Meteorological Department issued red alerts for Mumbai, Thane, Raigad, and Pune, warning of continued heavy rain and gusty winds up to 70 km/h.
  • Flights were disrupted at Mumbai airport, the Mumbai-Pune Expressway was closed, and local train services faced significant delays due to waterlogging.
  • The disaster is the latest in a string of deadly monsoon incidents that have killed dozens across Mumbai since early July.

At least six people were killed and two others injured when a landslide struck Mumbai's Kurla area on Tuesday, the latest deadly consequence of relentless monsoon rains that have battered India's financial capital for weeks. Rescue teams recovered victims from the debris as emergency services worked to secure the area and evacuate nearby residents.

The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) confirmed the casualties and deployed fire brigade, police, and civic staff to the site. The landslide occurred as continuous heavy rainfall destabilized hillside terrain, sending soil and debris crashing into residential structures in the densely populated neighborhood.

Red Alert as Mumbai Reels

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a red warning for Mumbai, Thane, Raigad, and Pune, predicting intense rainfall with gusty winds reaching speeds of 60 to 70 km/h. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis chaired a high-level meeting at the Disaster Control Room in Mantralaya to review the situation.

"People from landslide-prone areas have been evacuated," Fadnavis told reporters, warning that heavy rain combined with high tides could worsen waterlogging across the city. Schools and colleges were ordered closed as a precautionary measure.

The BMC reported receiving hundreds of complaints of tree falls, wall collapses, and structural damage across the city. Multiple neighborhoods including Sion, Chembur, Andheri, and Kurla reported knee-deep waterlogging, with major arterial roads rendered impassable.

Transport Infrastructure Paralyzed

The downpour brought Mumbai's transport network to its knees. The expressway connecting Mumbai to Pune — a critical commercial corridor — was shut after landslides sent construction rubble and debris onto the road. Television images showed broken slabs blocking lanes and water pouring from tunnel roofs, according to Reuters.

Flight operations at Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport were disrupted, with several airlines, including IndiGo, issuing advisories urging passengers to check flight status before traveling. Long-distance train services between Mumbai and Pune were cancelled, and local trains ran 15 to 20 minutes behind schedule as waterlogging affected tracks in multiple areas.

The Andheri subway was closed due to water accumulation, and vehicles were stranded on the Western Express Highway, leaving commuters with few options.

A Grim Pattern Repeats

The Kurla landslide is the latest in a series of deadly monsoon incidents across Mumbai this season. In early July, six people — including five children — were killed when multi-storey buildings collapsed in the Mankhurd area of eastern Mumbai. A separate landslide in Vikhroli in August killed two members of the Mishra family after a hillock collapsed onto their home at 2:39 a.m.

The monsoon season, which runs from June through September, brings most of South Asia's annual rainfall and is critical for agriculture. But it also devastates urban areas where poor drainage, hillside construction, and aging infrastructure amplify the damage from heavy rains.

"Mumbai will have high tide from 3 pm onwards today. If it rains heavily during the time of high tide, we will experience waterlogging."

— Devendra Fadnavis, Chief Minister, Maharashtra

Mumbai, home to over 20 million people, receives some of the heaviest rainfall of any major city during the monsoon. Some areas recorded more than 200 mm of rain in a single day during recent downpours, with Vikhroli logging 248.5 mm over 21 hours. The city's strained drainage infrastructure, much of it dating to the colonial era, struggles to handle such volumes.

With the IMD forecasting continued heavy rainfall in the coming days, officials have urged residents in low-lying and landslide-prone areas to remain vigilant and comply with evacuation orders.
